raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 12-year-old girl presented to our hospital with a headache of 3 days duration on March 23, 2019. The patient liked eating roasted seafood. Three days before hospitalization, the patient had had a fever (38-39 C), and a continuous headache with nausea but no vomiting. She had no myotonia or convulsion. She was referred to the Pediatric Neurology Unit of Hue Central Hospital with a headache of unknown cause and was examined by routine tests (as shown in Table 1). Her white blood cell (WBC) count was 5,450 cells/muL with 5.1% eosinophils. Chest radiography findings were normal, and computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain were unremarkable. A lumbar puncture was done and revealed 468 WBCs (65% neutrophils, 35% lymphocytes) and a CSF protein level of 0.63 g/L. The patient was treated for bacterial meningitis according to the European Society for Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases guideline with antibiotics such as vancomycin 60 mg/kg/day (March 26 to April 4), ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day (March 26 to April 2), and meropenem 100 mg/kg/day (April 3 to April 4). The patient's headache persisted, and a second lumbar puncture performed 7 days later demonstrated 750 WBCs (10% neutrophils, 90% lymphocytes), a CSF glucose level of 2.2 mmol/L, and a CSF protein level of 0.75 mg/dL. CSF culture for bacteria yielded no growth. The serum findings of an evaluation for Entamoeba histolytica, cysticercus, Schistosoma sp., Toxocara, Echinococcus sp., Fasciola sp., Strongyloides stercoralis, Gnathostoma sp., Ancylostoma caninum, Toxoplasma gondii, Paragonimus sp., Trichinella spiralis, and Helicobacter pylori were normal, and the serum ELISA tests of E. histolytica, cysticercus, Schistosoma sp., Toxocara, Echinococcus sp., Fasciola sp., S. stercoralis, Gnathostoma sp., A. caninum, T. gondii, Paragonimus sp., T. spiralis, and H. pylori were negative. Repeat lumbar puncture revealed 730 WBCs (10% lymphocytes, 5% neutrophils, and 65% eosinophils).
Given the presence of an eosinophilic pleocytosis in her spine, infection with A. cantonensis was suspected, and confirmation of A. cantonensis infection by immunodiagnosis was sought. Serum and CSF samples were sent to the Hospital for Tropical Diseases in Ho Chi Minh City (Vietnam), where Western blot analyses were done against A. cantonensis antigens. Both the serum and the CSF ELISA tests showed a strong reaction to A. cantonensis, confirming the diagnosis of angiostrongyliasis. The patient received treatment with albendazole (200 mg/day for 2 weeks), as well as intravenous dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg/day every 8 h) and mannitol (1.5 g/kg/day every 8 h) for the first 3 days, followed by 5 days of oral prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day). After 1 week of treatment, the patient's headache was relieved and the body temperature was normal. The last lumbar puncture performed on May 9, 2020, showed normal results.

subjective.chief_complaint: A previously healthy 12-year-old Vietnamese girl presented with a 3-day history of continuous headache, fever (38-39 C), and nausea without vomiting.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three days prior to hospitalization on March 23, 2019, the patient developed a continuous headache accompanied by fever (38-39 C) and nausea without vomiting, myotonia, or convulsions, prompting referral to the Pediatric Neurology Unit at Hue Central Hospital.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy child; dietary history remarkable for fondness for eating roasted seafood.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for continuous headache, fever (38-39 C), and nausea. Negative for vomiting, myotonia, or convulsions.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile (38-39 C) without convulsions or myotonia.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission peripheral blood count: WBC 5,450 cells/uL with 5.1% eosinophils. Chest radiograph was normal. Comprehensive serum evaluations and ELISA serologies for Entamoeba histolytica, Taenia solium (cysticercus), Schistosoma sp., Toxocara, Echinococcus sp., Fasciola sp., Strongyloides stercoralis, Gnathostoma sp., Ancylostoma caninum, Toxoplasma gondii, Paragonimus sp., Trichinella spiralis, and Helicobacter pylori were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: CT and MRI of the brain were unremarkable. First lumbar puncture (LP) showed CSF WBC 468 cells/uL (65% neutrophils, 35% lymphocytes) and protein 0.63 g/L. Second LP (day 7, for persistent headache despite empiric bacterial meningitis therapy) showed CSF WBC 750 cells/uL (10% neutrophils, 90% lymphocytes), glucose 2.2 mmol/L, protein 0.75 mg/dL, and negative CSF bacterial culture. Third repeat LP demonstrated marked CSF eosinophilic pleocytosis with 730 WBCs/uL (65% eosinophils, 10% lymphocytes, 5% neutrophils).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Paired serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) ELISA and Western blot assays performed at the Hospital for Tropical Diseases (Ho Chi Minh City) demonstrated a strong positive reaction against Angiostrongylus cantonensis antigens alongside marked CSF eosinophilic pleocytosis (65% eosinophils), confirming eosinophilic meningitis due to neural angiostrongyliasis (with bacterial meningitis and 13 other parasitic infections including Entamoeba histolytica ruled out). After failing initial empiric IV vancomycin (60 mg/kg/day), ceftriaxone (100 mg/kg/day), and meropenem (100 mg/kg/day), she was treated with oral albendazole (200 mg/day for 2 weeks), IV dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg/day divided q8h) and IV mannitol (1.5 g/kg/day divided q8h) for 3 days, followed by oral prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day for 5 days). Headache and fever resolved within 1 week, and a follow-up LP on May 9, 2020 was completely normal.
